CREATE PROCEDURE Website.SearchForSuppliers
@SearchText nvarchar(1000),
@MaximumRowsToReturn int
WITH EXECUTE AS OWNER
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT TOP(@MaximumRowsToReturn)
           s.SupplierID,
           s.SupplierName,
           c.CityName,
           s.PhoneNumber,
           s.FaxNumber ,
           p.FullName AS PrimaryContactFullName,
           p.PreferredName AS PrimaryContactPreferredName
    FROM Purchasing.Suppliers AS s
    INNER JOIN [Application].Cities AS c
    ON s.DeliveryCityID = c.CityID
    LEFT OUTER JOIN [Application].People AS p
    ON s.PrimaryContactPersonID = p.PersonID
    WHERE CONCAT(s.SupplierName, N' ', p.FullName, N' ', p.PreferredName) LIKE N'%' + @SearchText + N'%'
    ORDER BY s.SupplierName
    FOR JSON AUTO, ROOT(N'Suppliers');
END;

notes: WITH EXECUTE AS OWNER has no direct PostgreSQL equivalent; omitted (where the source declares it).

LIKE is translated by tsql_compat.like_to_regex into a case-insensitive regular expression: PostgreSQL LIKE has no [..] classes and treats backslash as an escape, SQL Server LIKE has no escape character. Patterns that the harness generates are checked; collation-specific equivalences outside them (for example ß = ss) are not claimed.

ORDER BY uses a tailored ICU collation (tsql_compat.latin1_general_100_ci_as: level 2, case-insensitive and accent-sensitive, ASCII punctuation order measured on SQL Server) plus removal of hyphens and apostrophes (Windows word sort), to follow the source's Latin1_General_100_CI_AS ordering. Verified for ASCII text; sort keys are generated distinct, so the order of ties is not claimed.
The JSON documents are compared as parsed values (key order, array order, nulls and strings are compared; whitespace is not).
@MaximumRowsToReturn is generated as 0..5; negative or NULL values (an error on SQL Server, not on PostgreSQL) are outside the property.

Step 4 is missed on the 5,000-row synthetic volume. Measured 2026-11-12: about 31-34 ms -> 18 ms after using ILIKE (no escape character) for patterns without '[' classes, -> 12-15 ms after enable_nestloop = off for the function (the planner expects the name search to keep almost no rows and looks up each city by index). SQL Server: 5-6 ms, so about 2.5x remains. What remains is the case-insensitive match over every concatenated name plus the sort; going under 1.5x would need an index on the searched text (e.g. pg_trgm), a schema change outside the conversion. Results are equivalent (step 3 passes); this is a performance finding, not a correctness one.

Verified in an isolated scratch database: the original T-SQL is deployed unchanged; tables contain only the columns the object references, with no foreign key constraints and no pre-existing rows. Every foreign-key column is indexed on both engines (a modelling assumption for the runtime step).
